notice: DEMO CORPUS — plain-language paraphrases compiled for the RoadSafe AI demo. Section IDs follow this demo compilation, not the official gazette numbering. Always verify against official sources before relying on any provision. Not legal advice.

documents.title: Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1965 — core driver duties (National framework, as applicable in Punjab)

sections.heading: Driving licence requirement
sections.text: No person may drive a motor vehicle in a public place without a valid driving licence for that class of vehicle. For a car or motorcycle the applicant must generally be at least 18 years old; learners must hold a learner permit and display the 'L' plate, and may not drive alone.

sections.heading: Documents to carry while driving
sections.text: A driver must be able to produce, on demand by a traffic officer: the driving licence, the vehicle registration certificate, and proof of at least third-party insurance. Driving without these documents is an offence and the vehicle may be impounded.

sections.heading: Obey signals, signs and traffic officers
sections.text: Every driver must obey traffic signals, road signs, road markings and the directions of a traffic police officer on point duty. Where a traffic officer is directing traffic, the officer's directions override the signals.

sections.heading: Speed limits
sections.text: A driver must not exceed the speed limit posted for the road, and must slow down where conditions require: near schools, hospitals, junctions, pedestrian crossings, road works, and in fog, rain or dust. Where no limit is posted, drive at a speed from which you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

sections.heading: Dangerous driving
sections.text: Driving in a manner that is dangerous to the public — racing, weaving between vehicles, driving while unfit, or ignoring obvious hazards — is an offence. Dangerous driving that causes death or serious injury attracts much heavier penalties.

sections.heading: Alcohol and drugs
sections.text: Driving or attempting to drive while under the influence of alcohol or drugs is prohibited. Pakistan applies zero tolerance: there is no permitted drink-drive limit, and refusal of a test is itself an offence.

sections.heading: Mobile phones
sections.text: A driver must not use a hand-held mobile phone while the vehicle is moving. The phone may only be used when safely parked with the engine off, or through a proper hands-free mounting that does not require handling the device.

sections.heading: Seat belts
sections.text: The driver and front-seat passenger must wear seat belts where the vehicle is fitted with them. The driver is responsible for ensuring children are properly restrained and do not sit in a dangerous position.

sections.heading: Motorcycle helmets
sections.text: The rider and the pillion passenger of a motorcycle must wear a standards-compliant helmet securely fastened. Riding without a helmet is an offence for both riders and passengers.

sections.heading: Overtaking rules
sections.text: Overtake only on the right of the vehicle ahead and only when the way is clearly visible; never overtake at junctions, pedestrian crossings, bridges, curves or road crests, and never exceed the speed limit while overtaking. The overtaken driver must not increase speed.

sections.heading: Keep left
sections.text: Pakistan drives on the left. Every vehicle must keep as far to the left side of the road as practicable; the right side is used to pass, and the extreme right lane of a dual carriageway is for overtaking only.

sections.heading: Pedestrian crossings
sections.text: A driver approaching a zebra or pedestrian crossing must slow down and must give way to pedestrians already on the crossing. Overtaking another vehicle that has stopped at a crossing is prohibited.

sections.heading: Duty after an accident
sections.text: A driver involved in an accident must stop, give whatever help is needed (especially to anyone injured), exchange name and vehicle details, and report the accident to police as soon as reasonably practicable. A seriously injured person should not be moved unless leaving them would be more dangerous; call Rescue 1122.

sections.heading: Insurance requirement
sections.text: Every motor vehicle used in a public place must carry at least third-party insurance covering injury or damage caused to other people and their property.

sections.heading: Overloading and passengers
sections.text: Carrying more passengers than the vehicle is registered for, or loads that are unsafe or obstruct the driver's view, is prohibited. A motorcycle may carry at most one pillion passenger.

sections.heading: Parking and stopping prohibitions
sections.text: Do not stop or park at pedestrian crossings, junctions, bridges, tunnels, bus stops, or where the kerb is marked yellow, and never double-park. Parking is only allowed where it does not obstruct or endanger other road users.

sections.heading: Penalties
sections.text: Fines and points for each offence are set out in the official schedule of penalties, which the federal and provincial governments amend from time to time. This demo corpus deliberately does not quote amounts — check the current official schedule or your traffic police website.

documents.title: Motorway (M-tag) traffic rules — National Highways & Motorway Police

sections.heading: Who may use the motorway
sections.text: Only motor vehicles capable of sustaining the minimum speed may use the motorway. Pedestrians, bicycles, rickshaws, animal-drawn vehicles and animals are prohibited. Learner drivers may not drive on the motorway.

sections.heading: Motorway speed limits
sections.text: For light cars the motorway minimum is 60 km/h and the maximum is 120 km/h; heavier vehicles have lower maxima. In fog, rain or other advisory conditions the posted limits are reduced and must be obeyed.

sections.heading: Motorway lane discipline
sections.text: Keep left except when overtaking, return to the left lane after passing, and do not use the hard shoulder as a driving lane — it is for emergencies only. Overtaking from the left is not allowed.

sections.heading: Breakdowns and stopping on the motorway
sections.text: Never stop on the carriageway. If the vehicle fails, move to the hard shoulder or a lay-by, switch on hazard lights, place a warning triangle well behind the vehicle (about 100 m on a motorway), stand away from traffic behind the barrier and call the Motorway Police helpline 130 or Rescue 1122.

sections.heading: Fog and low visibility on the motorway
sections.text: In fog: reduce speed well below the limit, use low-beam headlights with fog lamps, increase the gap to the vehicle ahead, follow overhead message signs, and never use high beams (the light reflects back). The Motorway Police may escort vehicles in convoy or temporarily close the motorway.

sections.heading: No U-turns or reversing
sections.text: U-turns, reversing and driving across the median are prohibited on the motorway. If you miss your exit, continue to the next interchange.

sections.heading: Fatigue and rest stops
sections.text: Drivers should rest at least every two hours on long journeys, using service areas and rest houses. Driving while drowsy on the motorway is treated as dangerous driving.

sections.heading: Steady red light
sections.text: A steady red light means STOP behind the white stop line — do not enter the junction. You must remain stopped until the light turns green. Turning on red is not permitted unless a sign at that junction expressly allows it.

sections.heading: Steady amber (yellow) light
sections.text: A steady amber light means the signal is about to turn red: stop before the stop line if you can do so safely. If you are already too close to stop safely, continue with caution and clear the junction without accelerating.

sections.heading: Steady green light
sections.text: A green light means proceed with care: give way to pedestrians still on the crossing and to any vehicle already inside the junction. Do not enter a junction if traffic ahead is not moving (keep clear), even on green.

sections.heading: Green arrow
sections.text: A green arrow gives a protected right of way only for the movement shown by the arrow (for example, a right-turn arrow). Conflicting traffic faces red during the arrow phase, but you must still yield to pedestrians on the crossing.

sections.heading: Red arrow
sections.text: A red arrow means the movement it points to is not allowed. Wait for the green arrow before making that turn, even if the main light is green for going straight.

sections.heading: Flashing red light
sections.text: A flashing red light works like a stop sign: come to a complete stop before the stop line, look both ways, yield to traffic and pedestrians, then proceed only when it is safe. Flashing red is commonly used at night and at low-traffic junctions.

sections.heading: Flashing amber (yellow) light
sections.text: A flashing amber light means proceed with caution: slow down, look, and give way where necessary. It does not mean stop, but you remain responsible for safe passage.

sections.heading: Pedestrian signals
sections.text: A steady WALK (green man) means pedestrians may start crossing; a flashing or countdown DON'T WALK means do not start — finish clearing if already on the crossing; a steady DON'T WALK (red man) means do not enter. Drivers must respect the parallel pedestrian phase.

sections.heading: Signal blackout or failure
sections.text: If signals are off or stuck on all-red flash, treat the junction as an all-way stop: stop, take turns in the order you arrived, and yield to the vehicle on your right when in doubt. Where a traffic officer is present, follow the officer.

sections.heading: Traffic officer overrides signals
sections.text: Hand signals and directions of a traffic warden or police officer on duty override the traffic lights. Follow the officer even when the lights say otherwise.

sections.heading: Right of way at junctions without lights
sections.text: At an unsignalized junction, yield to traffic approaching from your right and to vehicles already in the junction. At a T-junction, traffic on the continuing (through) road has priority.

sections.heading: Roundabout rules
sections.text: Pakistan traffic circulates clockwise at roundabouts: keep left on approach, yield to traffic already on the roundabout coming from your right, enter when there is a safe gap, do not stop inside the roundabout, and signal before your exit. Large vehicles may use the full width — give them room.

sections.heading: Regulatory signs — what they look like and mean
sections.text: Regulatory signs are compulsory. An octagon reading STOP means stop and give way; an inverted triangle means GIVE WAY; a red ring (circle) means a prohibition (e.g. a speed limit number, no entry, no overtaking); a blue circle means a mandatory instruction (e.g. keep left). Ignoring a regulatory sign is an offence.

sections.heading: Warning signs
sections.text: Warning signs are red-bordered triangles alerting you to hazards ahead — junctions, pedestrian crossings, schools, cattle, slippery roads, falling rocks, road narrowing, roundabouts ahead. Slow down when you see one.

sections.heading: Information and direction signs
sections.text: Rectangular blue signs give information and services (hospital, fuel, parking); green rectangular signs give directions and distances; motorway signs are blue with white text and symbols.

sections.heading: School zones and crossings
sections.text: Near schools and marked crossings, reduce speed well below the limit, never overtake, and be ready to stop for children. Some school zones post a lower limit during school hours — that posted limit applies.

sections.heading: Road works and temporary signs
sections.text: At road works, temporary signs, cones and flagmen override the permanent signs. Follow the reduced limits and the direction indicated; fines are often doubled for speeding through works zones.

sections.heading: Road markings basics
sections.text: A solid white stop line means stop at signals; zebra stripes mark pedestrian priority; arrows on the lane show permitted movements; a yellow kerb line means no stopping or parking; chevrons mark a hazard or sharp bend.
